Question 6. Exactly three output values

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Independently authored function question; no specific authentic source item is claimed for this mechanism.

How many functions from a five-element set to a four-element set have an image of size exactly three?

1.

600

2.

360

3.

240

4.

1024

Read the full derivation, conceptual proof and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 1.

Select attained labels, then require nonempty fibers. Choose three of the four target labels in (43)=4 ways. For a fixed chosen target set, the number of onto maps from five labelled inputs is

35−3·25+3·15=243−96+3=150.

The omission events overlap at constant functions, which explains the restoring term. The selected target set is the unique image of the function, so different selections cannot produce the same function. Multiply to obtain 4·150=600, option 1.

A second derivation. Onto maps to three labels have fiber profiles 3,1,1 or 2,2,1. For a fixed image set these contribute 3·5!/3!=60 and 3·5!/(2!2!)=90, totalling 150. Across four image sets this again gives 600.

Options. Option 4 gives 45=1024, which includes functions with one, two or four image values. Options 2 and 3 give 360 and 240; neither equals four copies of the exact fixed-image count 150. In fact 240 is the number of surjections onto all four targets, 4!(52)=240, a different image-size requirement.

Transfer. With m inputs and n target labels, image size k has count (nk)k!S(m,k). Choosing the image alone does not specify assignments to its members; ordering already labelled fibers again would overcount.

Question 7. Number of sections of a fixed map

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Independently authored function question; no specific authentic source item is claimed for this mechanism.

A surjection has three fibers of sizes 2, 3, and 4. How many right inverses g satisfy f∘g=id?

1.

9

2.

24

3.

12

4.

36

Read the full derivation, conceptual proof and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 2.

A right inverse is one representative per fiber. Write the three target labels as a,b,c. The identity f(g(a))=a forces g(a) into the two-element a-fiber. Independently g(b) must lie in the three-element b-fiber, and g(c) in the four-element c-fiber. The fibers are disjoint, so these choices automatically make g injective. Each selection yields one and only one reverse function satisfying the identity.

The product rule gives 2·3·4=24, option 2. Nine is the sum 2+3+4 and counts domain elements, not independent selections. Twelve omits the two choices in the first fiber, using only 3·4. Thirty-six is 3·3·4, which incorrectly supplies a third available representative in the explicitly two-element first fiber.

Verify a representative choice. If chosen inputs are a1,b2,c4, composition sends each target through its own chosen antecedent and back to itself. Choosing a2 instead changes g while preserving the identity. Every right inverse arises in this way because the identity forces membership in the named fibers.

Boundary. If any target fiber were empty, no right inverse could exist. These non-singleton fibers also show why none of the 24 sections is a true inverse of f: for example, both a-fiber inputs have the same f-value, so g cannot recover both of them.

This model uses this question’s finite types, fixed constraints or explicitly named counterexample. Representative cases are distinguished from exhaustive enumerations.

Question 8. Weakly increasing with fixed endpoints

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Independently authored function question; no specific authentic source item is claimed for this mechanism.

Count weakly increasing functions f:{1,…,6}→{1,2,3,4} with f(1)=1 and f(6)=4.

1.

15

2.

35

3.

56

4.

70

Read the full derivation, conceptual proof and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 2.

Account for the fixed endpoints before counting. The monotone output sequence has six positions and four possible values. Let cj be the multiplicity of j. The first endpoint being 1 forces c1≥1; the last being 4 forces c4≥1. Values 2 and 3 may be absent. Subtract one from the first and fourth counts. Four nonnegative residual counts now sum to 6−2=4.

Stars and bars gives (4+4−14−1)=(73)=35, so option 2 is correct. Equivalently, the four interior positions can be any weakly increasing sequence from four values; attach the prescribed endpoints to recover the full function.

Options. Fifteen is (62), the count for four interior positions using only three values; it discards an allowed value. Fifty-six is (83), obtained by imposing only the first endpoint and leaving five interior/residual positions. Seventy is twice 35, but the endpoint order is already fixed as 1 then 4 and has no extra two-way choice.

Concrete check. The function with output tuple (1,1,1,1,1,4) is legal and has residual multiplicities (4,0,0,0). The tuple (1,2,2,3,3,4) is also legal. Requiring every target to occur would incorrectly remove the first example and count only positive multiplicities.

Question 9. An idempotent map with two fixed points

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Independently authored function question; no specific authentic source item is claimed for this mechanism.

On a five-element set, how many functions have exactly two fixed points and satisfy f∘f=f?

1.

40

2.

80

3.

160

4.

20

Read the full derivation, conceptual proof and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 2.

Idempotence identifies the image with the fixed set. If y=f(x), the identity f(f(x))=f(x) says f(y)=y. Conversely every fixed point is an image point. Thus exactly two fixed points means exactly two image points, both fixed.

Choose their unordered two-element set in (52)=10 ways. Their outputs are forced to themselves. Each of the other three labelled inputs independently chooses one of those two points, giving 23=8 assignments. The total is 10·8=80, option 2. Every constructed map is idempotent because one application reaches a fixed point; every idempotent map with this image arises exactly once.

Question 10. Which composition implication survives?

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Independently authored function question; no specific authentic source item is claimed for this mechanism.

f:A→B and g:B→C are arbitrary maps. Which implication is always correct?

1.

If g∘f is injective, g is injective.

2.

If g∘f is surjective, f is surjective.

3.

If g∘f is bijective, f is injective and g is surjective.

4.

If f is surjective, g∘f is injective.

Read the full derivation, conceptual proof and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 3.

Track what a composite can actually detect. If g∘f is injective and f(a)=f(a'), applying g gives equal composite outputs. Composite injection forces a=a', proving f injective. If the composite is onto C, every c∈C equals g(f(a)) for some a; therefore c is an output of g, proving g onto. A bijective composite has both properties, so option 3 holds universally.

Reject option 1 with a typed counterexample. Let A={0}, B={b,c} and C={u}; set f(0)=b and g(b)=g(c)=u. The singleton composite is injective, but g has a collision.

Reject option 2. With the same maps the composite is onto the singleton C, but f misses c. Onto-ness of the composite says the attained middle points cover all final targets, not all middle targets.

Reject option 4. Let A=B={0,1}, take f to be the identity and g to be the constant map into C={u}. Then f is onto while the composite merges the two inputs and is not injective.

Sharpen the theorem. Composite injectivity is equivalent to f injective together with g injective on f[A]. Composite surjectivity is equivalent to g[f[A]]=C. The full unused part of B is precisely where reverse inferences can fail.

Question 12. Preimages and images behave differently

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Independently authored function question; no specific authentic source item is claimed for this mechanism.

For any f:A→B and subsets X,Y⊆A, which statement always holds?

1.
f(X∩Y)=f(X)∩f(Y)
2.
f(X∖Y)=f(X)∖f(Y)
3.
f(X∪Y)=f(X)∪f(Y)
4.
f(X)=f(Y)⇒X=Y
Read the full derivation, conceptual proof and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 3.

Images use existence of an antecedent. For any output b, membership in f[X∪Y] means that some input in X or Y maps to b. This is equivalent to membership in f[X]∪f[Y]. Both directions use the same witness, so option 3 is always true without injectivity or surjectivity.

One explicit collision diagnoses the other options. Let A={u,v}, B={b} and f(u)=f(v)=b. Set X={u} and Y={v}. The sets are disjoint, so f[X∩Y]=∅, while f[X]∩f[Y]={b}. Option 1 fails because its two output witnesses are different inputs.

For option 2, X∖Y=X, hence its image is {b}. But f[X]∖f[Y]=∅. A point outside Y can share an output with a point inside Y; subtraction after taking images loses that value.

For option 4, both images equal {b} although X≠Y. Equal output sets do not recover the input sets when collisions exist.

Exact recovery conditions. Injection makes the intersection and difference identities valid for every pair of input subsets, because equal output witnesses must then be the same input. Preimages of target subsets preserve these set operations for every total function: they test one fixed input's value and introduce no competing witnesses.

Question 13. Count involutions by their two-cycles

How many bijections on a five-element set satisfy f2=id and have exactly one fixed point?

15

2.

30

3.

4.

Read the full derivation, conceptual proof and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 1.

The identity after two applications restricts cycle lengths. A permutation satisfying f2=id has only fixed points and transpositions. With exactly one fixed point on five labels, the other four must form exactly two disjoint transpositions.

Choose the fixed label in five ways. For the other four, choose a partner for their smallest label in three ways; the remaining pair is then forced. Equivalently the pairing count is 4!/(22·2!)=3, dividing by within-pair order and by order of the two pairs. Hence the total is 5·3=15, option 1.

Options. Thirty omits division by the order of the two disjoint pairs: 5·4!/22=30. Sixty omits both pair-order division and one within-pair division: 5·4!/2=60. Forty-five would require nine distinct pairings for each fixed point; the explicit partner construction proves there are exactly three, excluding it.

Concrete list for one fixed point. If label 5 is fixed, the possible pairings are (12)(34), (13)(24), and (14)(23). Rewriting (12) as (21), or exchanging the displayed pair order, does not change the function. This is why the divisions are required.

Boundary. The number of nonfixed labels in any involution must be even. Five labels can have one, three or five fixed points, but not two. Longer cycles cannot satisfy the squared-identity condition.

Derive the count or structural law. Order the three labelled inputs once. Their distinct outputs have n+3, then n+2, then n+1 possibilities. Multiplication gives the falling product. Surjectivity and overlapping omissions

Question 18. Surjectivity and overlapping omissions — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Independently authored function question; no specific authentic source item is claimed for this mechanism.

60
2.
150
3.
243
4.
147
Read the full derivation, conceptual proof and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 2.

Derive the count or structural law. Let E_a,E_b,E_c denote tuples missing a specified target. There are 3n unrestricted tuples and 2n in each event. Each pair of missed-target events has one constant tuple for positive n. There are three such pairs. Their triple intersection is empty because a nonempty domain has no function into an empty target. Inclusion–exclusion therefore gives 3n−3·2n+3. A constant tuple is removed twice in the first subtraction and restored once, leaving zero net count; an onto tuple is untouched.

Substitute the stated parameter. At n=5 the law gives 3(5)−3·2(5)+3=150. Every label and every constraint is retained from the stem.

Compute all alternatives. Option 1 gives 3!((5)3)=60; it chooses one distinguished antecedent per target without specifying the other outputs, and may select the same completed function many times. Option 2 gives 150, equal to the derived result. Option 3 gives 3(5)=243; it counts all output tuples, including those that miss a target. Option 4 gives 3(5)−3·2(5)=147; it subtracts constant maps twice without restoring the overlaps.

Boundary and transfer. At n=1 and n=2 the count is zero, consistent with the finite size obstruction. The positive-domain formula must not be used at n=0 without the triple-intersection term; there the onto count is zero, not one.

Boundary and transfer. The formula uses n≥1. At n=1 there is one fixed-point cycle; at n=2 there is one transposition. An n-cycle has order n, while a permutation with several cycles has order equal to the least common multiple of their lengths.

Derive the count or structural law. The two distinguished points have their outputs forced to themselves. No other input may use those two targets because a permutation is injective. Thus the remaining n−2 input labels must biject to the remaining n−2 target labels, with (n−2)! choices. Additional fixed points among those remaining labels are allowed. Every such remaining permutation extends uniquely by the two fixed assignments.

Substitute the stated parameter. At n=5 the law gives ((5)−2)!=6. Every label and every constraint is retained from the stem.

Compute all alternatives. Option 1 gives 6, equal to the derived result. Option 2 gives ((5)−1)!=24; it forces only one specified point to be fixed and leaves the second unconstrained. Option 3 gives (5)!=120; it permutes the two prescribed fixed points as well as the other labels. Option 4 gives ((5)2)=10; it chooses which labels to fix although those labels are already specified, and omits the remaining permutation.

Boundary and transfer. The two specified distinct points require n≥2. At n=2 the identity is the unique map. Choosing exactly two unspecified fixed points would instead give (n2)Dn−2; the choice factor belongs to that different task.

n!

Read the full derivation, conceptual proof and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 3.

Derive the count or structural law. The two distinguished points have their outputs forced to themselves. No other input may use those two targets because a permutation is injective. Thus the remaining n−2 input labels must biject to the remaining n−2 target labels, with (n−2)! choices. Additional fixed points among those remaining labels are allowed. Every such remaining permutation extends uniquely by the two fixed assignments.

Universal expression. The bijective construction gives (n−2)!, option 3, throughout the stated domain where the required objects exist. The result is not extrapolated from one successful numerical example.

Compare the other laws. The alternative n! permutes the two prescribed fixed points as well as the other labels. At n=5 it gives 120, whereas the required count is 6. The alternative (n2) chooses which labels to fix although those labels are already specified, and omits the remaining permutation. At n=5 it gives 10, whereas the required count is 6. The alternative (n−1)! forces only one specified point to be fixed and leaves the second unconstrained. At n=5 it gives 24, whereas the required count is 6. A numerical disagreement disproves a competing expression asserted for every valid parameter; agreement at a degenerate parameter would not establish that universal claim.

Boundary and transfer. The two specified distinct points require n≥2. At n=2 the identity is the unique map. Choosing exactly two unspecified fixed points would instead give (n2)Dn−2; the choice factor belongs to that different task.

Question 45. Specified fixed points versus exactly two fixed points — applicability and boundary

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Independently authored function question; no specific authentic source item is claimed for this mechanism.

Count permutations on an n -element set that fix two specified distinct points; other fixed points are allowed. Which statement correctly identifies the scope or a failure of this method? Assume n≥2.

1.

Choosing the fixed points completes the permutation.

2.

Exactly two fixed points would require a derangement on the remaining points.

3.

Fixing two specified points means no other point may be fixed.

4.

The two specified points can exchange their images.

Read the full derivation, conceptual proof and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 2.

Derive the count or structural law. The two distinguished points have their outputs forced to themselves. No other input may use those two targets because a permutation is injective. Thus the remaining n−2 input labels must biject to the remaining n−2 target labels, with (n−2)! choices. Additional fixed points among those remaining labels are allowed. Every such remaining permutation extends uniquely by the two fixed assignments.

Check each scope claim. Option 1: Once the prescribed two assignments are fixed, the remaining labels can still be permuted. For n=4 the two residual labels may remain fixed or be exchanged. Option 2: If no additional fixed points are allowed, the residual permutation must have no fixed point, so the count becomes the derangement number D_{n−2}. Option 3: The identity fixes the two prescribed points and also every other point. It is a legal map under the question as written. Option 4: Exchanging the prescribed points sends each to the other and contradicts the two required fixed assignments. Their outputs are not free. Thus option 2 is correct.

Boundary and transfer. The two specified distinct points require n≥2. At n=2 the identity is the unique map. Choosing exactly two unspecified fixed points would instead give (n2)Dn−2; the choice factor belongs to that different task.

Question 46. All idempotent maps on four points

Original integrated challenge · retained after review

How many total functions on a four-element labelled set satisfy f∘f=f?

1.
24
2.
36
3.
41
4.
64
Read the full derivation, conceptual proof and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 3.

Count by the exact fixed image. An idempotent endofunction fixes exactly its image. For image size k on four labelled elements, choose that image in (4k) ways; its assignments are fixed. The remaining 4−k inputs independently choose from those k outputs, giving k4−k maps for the chosen image. Different image sets and different image sizes are disjoint cases.

The nonempty domain prohibits an empty image. Sum the four allowed sizes:

(41)13+(42)22+(43)31+(44)40=4+24+12+1=41.

Option 3 is correct. Twenty-four counts only the maps with a two-element fixed image. Thirty-six combines the two-element and three-element cases but omits the four constant maps and the identity. Sixty-four is 43, a free-output count with no appropriate idempotence restriction.

Why the construction is exhaustive. If f is idempotent and y=f(x), then f(y)=y. Thus all nonimage points map into fixed image points, exactly as constructed. Conversely every construction has f(f(x))=f(x) at every x. This establishes necessity and sufficiency, rather than checking selected tuples only.

Generalization. For a nonempty n-element carrier, sum (nk)kn−k for k=1 through n. The empty carrier has one empty idempotent map and must be treated separately from a sum with no nonempty image cases.

Question 47. Count split inverse pairs

Original integrated challenge · retained after review

A has two labelled elements and B three. How many ordered function pairs f:A→B, g:B→A satisfy g∘f=idA?

1.
6
2.
8
3.
12
4.
18
Read the full derivation, conceptual proof and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 3.

The composition identity first forces f to be injective. If f(a)=f(a'), applying g and using g∘f=idA gives a=a'. There are 3·2=6 injections from the two labelled A-elements into three labelled B-elements.

For each such f, the values of g on the two attained B-points are forced by their unique antecedents. At the sole unused B-point, g may independently choose either A-point. Thus each f has exactly two left inverses. Multiply to get 6·2=12, option 3.

Example. If A={0,1}, B={a,b,c}, f(0)=a and f(1)=b, then g(a)=0 and g(b)=1 are forced; g(c)=0 or 1 gives the two pairs belonging to this f. No noninjective f can appear because it would violate the first argument.

Options. Six counts the injections but omits the two possible reverse maps. Eight counts all 23 reverse assignments for a fixed B without imposing their dependence on a chosen f. Eighteen is 32·2 and incorrectly lets f have collisions. The ordered pair (f,g) includes both functions, so counting only one factor is insufficient.

Transfer. For m>0 and n≥m, the number of pairs f:A→B,g:B→A with the left identity is n!/(n−m)!mn−m. If A is empty and B nonempty, the forward map exists but no reverse total map exists; the pair count is zero. If both are empty, the unique empty pair satisfies the identity.

Chapter summary and detailed examination decisions

Throughout this section, m is the finite domain size and n the finite codomain size. These meanings do not change between formulas. A summary supports the full proofs; it does not replace them. The rules describe mathematical applicability rather than an unmeasured frequency of examination appearances.

1. Validate a prescription before classifying it

A total declaration f:A→B requires exactly one B-output for every A-input. The rule x↦1/x on all reals fails at zero; the square-root rule on a real domain fails at negative inputs. Calling either declaration noninjective does not address this validity failure. Repair the domain or rule explicitly before discussing its image.

2. Include all empty-type cases

An empty-domain function into each fixed B is unique and injective. It is onto only when B is empty. A nonempty A has no total map into an empty B. Thus total-map counts use the combinatorial convention 00=1, reflecting the unique empty graph. A left inverse of ∅→{b} would have an impossible reverse type.

3. Domain and codomain belong to the function

The square rule on reals to reals has collisions and misses negative targets. Restricted to nonnegative reals and corestricted to nonnegative reals it is bijective. Changing the codomain affects onto-ness, while changing the domain may eliminate collisions or outputs. The formula alone does not determine the answer. Equal typed functions must also have matching declared types.

4. Use fibers as certificates

The fibers Fb={a:f(a)=b} are disjoint and cover A. An oversized fiber certifies a collision; an empty target fiber certifies a missed target. Injection means sizes at most one, surjection sizes at least one. For output tuple (a,a,b,c) into {a,b,c,d}, the a-fiber has two members and the d-fiber none, certifying both failures.

5. State the finite-size hypothesis

For finite sets, injection implies m≤n and surjection m≥n. At m=n either property implies bijectivity. On infinite naturals, the shift n↦n+1 is injective and not onto, so the reverse implication fails. Equality of cardinalities asserts existence of some bijection; a specified constant map between equal finite carriers can still fail both properties.

6. Count total maps before imposing extra conditions

For labelled inputs and outputs, each of m inputs independently chooses one of n targets, giving nm. Four inputs and three targets give 34=81. No division by input or target permutations is justified because labels distinguish functions. This count includes collisions and missed targets; onto or injective conditions require separate counting.

7. Count injections with distinct choices

For m≤n, successive outputs have n,n−1,…,n−m+1 possibilities, giving n!/(n−m)!. If m>n the count is zero. Three inputs into eight targets give 8·7·6=336. Choosing their image gives only (83)=56 sets; each admits 3!=6 assignments to the input labels. Equal-size bijections number m!.

8. Onto counts restore overlap

For positive m,n, onto maps number ∑j=0n(−1)j(nj)(n−j)m. Omission events overlap at tuples missing several targets; subtracting them without restoration is wrong. Six inputs onto four targets give 4096−2916+384−4=1560. Divide by 30 only if that is the requested transformed quantity; here the quotient is 52.

9. Image size is a two-stage choice

Exactly k attained targets give (nk)k!S(m,k). Choose the labelled image set and then require a surjection to it. Five inputs with three attained labels among four give 4(243−96+3)=600. Choosing the image alone leaves outputs unspecified. Multiplying again by k! after an onto count already using labels would count those labels twice.

10. A prescribed fiber is selected and then excluded elsewhere

If one named target has exactly r antecedents, choose those inputs and keep that target unavailable at every remaining input: (mr)(n−1)m−r. With m=7,n=3,r=3 the result is 35·16=560. This does not require the other targets nonempty. Additional onto-ness changes the residual output count.

11. Fiber-size vectors carry target labels

For prescribed labelled sizes summing to m, the count is m!/∏rj!. A profile without assigned target labels needs a separate profile-assignment factor. For onto six-to-four maps, profiles (3,1,1,1) and (2,2,1,1) contribute 480 and 1080. Equal profile sizes do not make the input assignments unlabelled; never divide their multinomial count by n!.

12. Partial functions add a fresh undefined choice

An m-input, n-output partial function independently selects n outputs or undefinedness at each input, giving (n+1)m. Exactly k defined inputs give (mk)nk. If n=0 the only partial map is everywhere undefined. A sentinel must lie outside the ordinary target, or a defined sentinel-valued output would be confused with undefinedness.

13. Monotone maps are multiplicity vectors

Weakly increasing maps from m ordered inputs into n ordered values correspond to n nonnegative counts summing to m. They number (m+n−1n−1) for n>0. With m=n=5 the result is (94)=126. Repeated values and unused targets are permitted. Treating the outputs as distinct would solve a strict-increase problem instead.

14. Endpoint conditions consume only their own compulsory occurrences

For m,n≥2, first output 1 and last output n require positive multiplicities for those two labels, giving (m+n−3n−1). With m=6,n=4 this is (73)=35. Interior values need not occur. If all outputs are required, positive counts for every label give (m−1n−1) when m≥n.

15. Strict monotonicity has different finite and infinite consequences

Strictly increasing finite-chain maps choose distinct targets and number (nm). A strict self-map of a finite chain must be the identity. On integers, x↦x+1 preserves strict order and is not the identity. It still is injective. Retain the source statement's distinction between identity and injection and its absence of a finite-carrier hypothesis.

16. Follow the inside map first

For f:A→B and g:B→C, the rule is (g∘f)(a)=g(f(a)). Its source is A and target C. With f(x)=x+1 and g(x)=2x the two orders give 2x+2 and 2x+1. The inverse of a composite of bijections reverses this order. Composition is associative with compatible types, generally not commutative.

17. A rule composite must preserve the outer domain

For f(x)=x²−1 and g(t)=1/t, the composite excludes x=−1 and x=1. Simplification does not create a value at either point. More generally its allowable inputs satisfy f(x) in the domain of g. If declared intermediate types do not match but the inner image lies in the outer domain, insert the required restriction or corestriction explicitly.

18. A composite sees only the attained middle values

Composite injection forces f injective; composite onto-ness forces g onto. The stronger exact tests are injection of f and of g on f[A], or g[f[A]]=C respectively. An unused middle point can participate in a g-collision without spoiling the composite. Thus a bijective composite does not automatically make both factors bijective on their full types.

19. Extra composition hypotheses recover the missing implication

If the composite is bijective and f is onto, g's potential collisions can all be lifted to A and are excluded by composite injection. Both factors become bijective. If the composite is bijective and g injective, its onto-ness forces every B-point into f[A], again giving both bijections. Name the additional hypothesis instead of applying either theorem to arbitrary maps.

20. Cancellation is universally quantified

An injective outer g can be cancelled from g∘f=g∘h. An onto inner f can be cancelled from g∘f=h∘f. Converse characterizations compare all appropriately typed maps. A missed middle point hides a difference between outer maps; a collision hides a difference between inner maps. Equality for one pair of maps does not itself prove the cancelling function has the required property.

21. A true inverse requires both identities

An inverse h:B→A satisfies h∘f=idA and f∘h=idB. Solving y=f(x) supplies a candidate, which still needs correct types and both verifications. For x≤2 and f(x)=(x−2)²+3, the valid inverse branch is 2−y−3 on y≥3. A reciprocal and a preimage set are different operations.

22. Left inverses have unused-target freedom

For an injection with m>0, a left inverse is forced on f[A] but has m choices on each unused target. Thus its count is mn−m. A three-to-five injection has nine left inverses. These reverse maps are onto A, but generally not inverse to f in the other direction. For an empty domain and nonempty target no reverse total map exists.

23. Right inverses select one input from each fiber

A section of a fixed finite surjection has count ∏b|Fb|. Fibers 2,3,4 give 24 sections. Each section is injective because different targets have disjoint fibers. A section does not make the original f injective or recover unchosen antecedents. A missing fiber gives zero choices and forbids a right inverse.

24. Count split pairs with both factors present

For m>0 and n≥m, pairs with g∘f=idA number n!/(n−m)!mn−m. Two inputs and four middle targets give 48 pairs. The first factor chooses the injection and the second its free reverse values. Reversing the identity reverses the finite size condition. Requiring both identities gives only bijective pairs with a unique reverse map.

25. Idempotence fixes precisely the image

If f2=f and y=f(x), then f(y)=y. Conversely a fixed y belongs to the image. For exactly k image points on n nonempty labelled points, choose them and map every other input to one of them: (nk)kn−k. Two fixed points on five labels give 10·8=80. Two image values without idempotence need not be fixed.

26. Count all idempotents by disjoint image sizes

Sum (nk)kn−k for k=1,…,n on a nonempty carrier. For n=4 the contributions are 4,24,12,1, totalling 41. An empty image is impossible for a nonempty total domain. The empty carrier instead has one empty idempotent map. An idempotent injection or an idempotent surjection must be the identity, but idempotence alone gives neither property.

27. Involutions allow only cycles of lengths one and two

The squared identity makes every orbit length divide two. With j transpositions on n labels, the count is n!/[2jj!(n−2j)!]. Two transpositions on eight labels give 210; exactly two fixed points there instead means three transpositions and gives 420. Within-pair order and pair order are immaterial, while all labels remain distinguished.

28. Cyclic rotations are displays of the same function

A single cycle on n≥1 labelled points has (n−1)! arrangements: fix one start and order the remaining labels. For n=5 this is 24. Dividing n! by n removes redundant starting positions. Reversing a cycle of length at least three changes its successor function, so another universal division by two would be wrong. Length one and two are the reversal exceptions.

29. Specified fixed points are not exactly fixed points

Fixing two named points on n≥2 labels leaves (n−2)! residual permutations, with further fixed points permitted. Exactly two named fixed points instead requires a derangement on the residual labels. Exactly two unspecified fixed points adds the choice factor (n2). On five labels the first task gives six maps; the identity is among them and demonstrates why further fixed points cannot be excluded.

30. Direct images can merge different witnesses

Images preserve unions always. They satisfy f[X∩Y]⊆f[X]∩f[Y] and f[X]∖f[Y]⊆f[X∖Y] unconditionally. Distinct inputs u,v with f(u)=f(v) make both inclusions strict for disjoint singleton sets. Injection restores equality for all such set pairs. The direction of the difference inclusion must not be reversed.

31. Preimages preserve Boolean operations for every total function

For T,U⊆B, preimages preserve union, intersection, difference and complement relative to B and A. They test the single value f(a), so no competing witnesses are needed. Even a many-to-one function has these laws. A preimage exists without a true inverse and may have several inputs; f(x)=x² gives preimage {−2,2} for target singleton {4}.

32. Round trips measure saturation and unattained targets

The input round trip f−1[f[S]] fills entire touched fibers; equality with S holds exactly for saturated S. The target round trip is f[f−1[T]]=T∩f[A]. A two-input a-fiber expands either of its singleton subsets; an unused target disappears from the target round trip. Universal recovery on the two sides characterizes injection and surjection respectively.

33. Power-set operators interchange one classification

The direct-image operator is injective exactly when f is injective, and onto exactly when f is onto. The preimage operator is injective exactly when f is onto, and onto exactly when f is injective. An unused target gives two distinct target subsets with the same preimage; a collision makes an individual colliding input impossible as an entire preimage. These statements classify the operators, not an inverse of f.

34. Quotient descent must respect every representative

A rule [a]R↦[f(a)]S is well-defined exactly when aRa′ implies f(a)Sf(a′). Literal output equality is stronger and unnecessary if the target is a quotient. For [x]4↦[ax+b]6, the condition is 6∣4a, equivalent to 3 dividing a. Testing only the four selected representatives would overlook the equivalent pair 0,4 and cannot prove the condition.

35. Function spaces are constructed, not formally exponent-reassociated

Currying gives a bijection between CA×B and (CB)A by v(a)(b)=u(a,b). A map on a tagged union corresponds to a pair of component maps. But CBA generally differs: for |A|=3 and |B|=|C|=2 its size is 256, while (CB)A has size 64. Preserve the parentheses and actual input type.

36. Powers depend on cycle lengths and entry distances

For a nonempty finite endofunction let H be maximal cycle-entry distance and L the cycle-length least common multiple. A positive power f^k is idempotent exactly when k≥H and L divides k. In the tuple (1,2,2,4,3,4,5), H=L=2, so the square is idempotent; the third power still swaps a two-cycle. Reaching a cycle and fixing its phase are separate requirements.

37. Infinite encodings must be injective or surjective by proof

Decode 2x(2y+1)−1 by factoring z+1 into a power of two and an odd factor. This proves a bijection on zero-based natural pairs; replacing the exponent by multiplication destroys it. Schröder–Bernstein uses two injections to construct a new bijection, without making either original map onto. Finite examples of the layers illustrate its construction, while the general proof handles every input.

38. Distinguish a chosen enumeration from a given order

A bijective natural-number listing transports a well-order to any countably infinite set. The usual order on the integers still has no least element; countability does not make every existing order well-founded. Cantor's diagonal argument prohibits a surjection from A onto its power set, so no natural-number listing enumerates all binary sequences. These are existence and nonexistence statements with different quantifiers.

Interactive fiber laboratory

The laboratory below analyzes finite total functions. Choose one output for each of four labeled inputs, then inspect the fibers, collision witnesses, missed targets, saturation, and inverse eligibility. Use the presets to compare a bijection, an onto map with collisions, and an injection with an unused target. The selected subset demonstrates why a direct-image/preimage round trip can add inputs. It does not administer an assessment or record a performance score.

S is the subset selected in the last column. Changing an output or a selection recalculates the exact fibers and both subset operations immediately.
